title: Oil and the rupee: who pays when a barrel in the Gulf gets dearer
hook:
On an October afternoon in 2018, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley walked out to meet reporters with what sounded like good news. Petrol and diesel had been hitting records for weeks, the rupee was at its weakest ever, and voters were angry. So the government would cut excise duty on fuel, and it would ask the state oil companies to knock a further rupee off every litre themselves.

Drivers cheered. Shareholders of Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum did not. Before trading closed, the three stocks had crashed by double digits, and by some counts by around a fifth.

That afternoon is the whole of this chapter in miniature. When oil gets expensive, India does not get to decide whether to pay. It only gets to decide who pays: the driver at the pump, the government's budget, the oil companies' shareholders, or everyone, through a weaker rupee. Let's trace the chain, link by link.
short: India imports most of the crude it uses, so an oil spike hits through five channels at once: the current account, the rupee, inflation, the government's budget and company margins.

Services exports and remittances, India's two big structural surpluses, comfortably cover a normal oil bill but not a spike. The gap leans on fickle foreign portfolio money, and when that leaves, the RBI's defence of the rupee drains liquidity at home.

Somebody has to absorb the shock: drivers through pump prices, the government through lower excise and higher subsidies, or the state oil companies through losses. That split decides which stocks bleed.
Oil and rising US interest rates together are the worst pairing for India. They hit in 2013, 2018 and 2022, and they are hitting again now.

In our own data, only one sector result holds in every kind of oil spike: consumer staples lag. The rallies in metals and PSU banks came mostly from demand-led oil recoveries, not supply shocks like today's.

sections.heading: Why a barrel in the Gulf is India's problem
sections.html:
India is the world's third-largest oil consumer and produces only a small fraction of what it burns. The rest arrives by tanker, much of it from the Persian Gulf, and it has to be paid for in dollars. Crude oil is routinely the single largest item in India's import bill.

To see why that matters, think of the country as a household and its current account as the family's monthly budget with the outside world.

  • Salary in: what the country earns selling to foreigners. India's real strength is services: software, IT outsourcing and the global capability centres multinationals run out of Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
  • Money from family abroad: remittances. Millions of Indians working in the Gulf, America and Britain send money home. India is the world's largest recipient of remittances.
  • Spending out: imports. Oil, gold, electronics, coal, edible oil, machinery.

India buys far more goods than it sells, so the goods account runs a large deficit every year. Services and remittances plug most of that hole. In a normal year, with oil at a moderate price, the current account deficit, the gap left over, is small and easily financed.

But oil is the swing item. Gold and electronics move fairly predictably. Oil can jump by half in a few months because of a war thousands of kilometres away. When it does, the import bill balloons while software exports and remittances carry on as before. The household's salary has not changed, but the electricity bill has doubled.

Services and remittances pay for a normal oil bill. They were never built to pay for a war.

A deficit is not shameful in itself; a fast-growing country often imports more than it exports. The question is how the gap gets filled, and that is where the rupee comes in.

sections.heading: How an oil spike becomes a weaker rupee
sections.html:
Follow the dollars. When Indian Oil buys a cargo of Saudi or Iraqi crude, it has to pay in dollars. So it goes to its bank and buys dollars with rupees. Multiply that by every refiner, every month. When oil jumps, so does the demand for dollars, and the rupee's price falls.

On the other side, someone has to bring dollars into India to fill the gap. There are two kinds of foreign money.

  • Foreign direct investment: factories, stakes, offices. Sticky; nobody dismantles a plant because oil rose for a quarter.
  • Foreign portfolio investment: funds buying Indian shares and bonds. It can leave with a click, and tends to leave exactly when the world gets scary, which is often when oil is spiking.

So the cruel arithmetic of an oil shock is that the gap widens at the very moment the fickle half of its financing heads for the exit. Something has to give.

That something is either the rupee or the RBI's reserves. If the RBI lets the market clear, the rupee falls until imports look expensive enough and Indian assets cheap enough to balance things. If it resists, it sells dollars from its reserves. And as the chapter on the RBI explains, every dollar the RBI sells pulls rupees out of the banking system, tightening liquidity and pushing up interest rates at home. A currency defence is monetary tightening by another name.

There is a nasty loop here too. Oil is priced in dollars, so a weaker rupee makes every barrel more expensive in rupee terms, which widens the deficit further. In 2013, the RBI broke the loop by opening a special window to sell dollars directly to the three state oil companies, keeping their huge purchases off the open market. In October 2026 it opened a dollar window for oil companies again.

[[fig:1]]

The chart puts Brent on top and the rupee below, with the big episodes marked. Read the bottom line as a staircase rather than a slope. The long drift weaker is partly just India's higher inflation compared with America's. The steep steps come in 2018 and 2022, both oil years, and the record low arrived in July 2026, in the middle of the Iran war.

sections.heading: Who pays: the pump, the budget or the oil companies
sections.html:
Now the fiscal leg, which is where Indian oil shocks get politically interesting. When crude jumps, the extra cost has to land on someone. There are four main ways the government shuffles it around.

  • Pass it to the driver. Let pump prices rise. Cheap for the budget, but it feeds inflation and is deeply unpopular, so it rarely happens fully or fast.
  • Cut excise duty. A big part of the pump price is tax. Trimming it shields consumers and the inflation index, at the cost of revenue. The government did this in May 2022, and cut excise sharply again in March 2026 as the Iran war pushed crude above a hundred dollars.
  • Lean on the oil companies. Keep retail prices frozen and let Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum sell below cost. Their losses, called under-recoveries, are a subsidy the government does not have to put in its budget. Economists call this quasi-fiscal: a cost to the state hidden in a company's accounts.
  • Tax the winners. When crude is high, domestic producers like ONGC and Oil India earn windfalls, and refiners can make bumper margins exporting fuel. In July 2022 India imposed a windfall tax on domestic crude production and on fuel exports to claw some of that back.

Some costs are automatic. Urea is made largely from imported gas priced off oil, while farmers pay a fixed price, so the fertiliser subsidy rises with energy prices without anyone deciding anything.

Now you can see why economists talk about India's twin deficits. An oil shock widens the current account deficit, as we saw above, and the fiscal deficit at the same time, through lost excise, bigger subsidies and oil company losses the state eventually has to cover. Foreign bond investors and rating agencies watch the two together. When both widen at once, they demand higher yields to lend to India, and the rupee feels it.

Each choice picks a different loser: consumption, public spending on roads and railways, oil company shareholders or producers. There is no option in which nobody pays.

sections.heading: Inside company accounts: who bleeds and who gains
sections.html:
Crude is not just fuel; it is a raw material for much of industrial India, so a spike shows up in margins far beyond the pump.

The obvious losers. For an airline, jet fuel is the biggest single cost, and it is priced in dollars, so oil and the rupee hit twice. Paint companies use a long list of crude derivatives as raw materials. Tyre makers buy synthetic rubber and carbon black, both oil products. Specialty chemicals, plastics and packaging companies are similar. Cement makers burn petroleum coke and move heavy bags by diesel truck. All face the same squeeze: costs rise at once, price hikes take months.

The oil marketing companies are a special case. They earn money in two places: refining crude into fuel, and selling that fuel at their pumps. In a spike, refining margins can actually be fat. But if pump prices are frozen, the marketing arm loses money on every litre, and that usually swamps the refining gain. Their profits become a policy decision rather than a business outcome, which is why their shares swing on every government statement.

The quiet loser: staples. Soap, detergent, biscuits and edible oil companies buy palm oil, crude-linked chemicals and plastic packaging. With price-sensitive customers and fierce competition, they absorb costs for a while, and margins compress. At the same time, an oil shock lifts inflation and squeezes the household budgets that buy their products.

The winners. Upstream producers gain from higher crude, unless the government taxes away the windfall, which, as 2022 showed, it is willing to do. Exporters, such as IT services and pharmaceuticals, earn in dollars and gain from a weaker rupee. But only if the RBI lets the rupee fall. If it defends the currency, that cushion never arrives.

The borrowers. When the RBI sells dollars and money tightens, lenders that fund themselves in the bond market see costs rise. They lose from an oil shock without ever buying a barrel.

sections.heading: What our own data says, and the trap in it
sections.html:
So which sectors have actually done well or badly when oil rose fast? We ran the numbers ourselves. We took every three-month window since 2016 in which Brent rose by more than a quarter, and measured how each sector index did against the Nifty over the same window.

[[fig:2]]

Here's how to read it. Each bar is a sector's average return relative to the Nifty in those windows. Bars in full colour have a t-statistic of at least two and a half, which in plain terms means the result is strong enough that it is unlikely to be luck. Pale bars could easily be noise.

At first glance it looks like a playbook: metals, PSU banks and realty up, FMCG down. But here is the trap.

Oil can rise for two completely different reasons. In a demand-led rise, the world economy is recovering, factories are humming and everybody wants more energy. That is what happened in 2016, after the oil crash bottomed, and from mid-2020 into early 2021, after the Covid collapse. In those windows, metals, PSU banks and property rallied because the whole economic cycle was turning up. Oil was a symptom of good news.

In a supply-led rise, oil is expensive because barrels have stopped flowing: a war, an embargo, a blockade. That is pure bad news for an importer like India. Of all the windows in our sample, only 2022 and 2026 are supply shocks. Most of the data describes a different kind of event from today's.

Before you ask what oil is doing, ask why oil is doing it.

The one result that fits both kinds of shock is FMCG lagging the market. Whether oil rises because the world is booming or because a strait is closed, staples companies face input costs that climb faster than they can pass them on. That is the finding we would bet on. The metals and PSU bank bars, we would not.

sections.heading: Why oil plus US rates is the worst pairing
sections.html:
An oil shock on its own is painful but manageable: India has large reserves and a far bigger services surplus than in the 1990s. Real stress comes when it coincides with rising interest rates in America.

Here is why. When US Treasury yields rise, global investors can earn a handsome return in the safest asset in the world. The case for emerging-market risk weakens, money flows home and the dollar strengthens. So at the very moment India needs more foreign money to finance a bigger oil bill, the global pool of that money is shrinking.

This is the pattern of every serious rupee episode of the last fifteen years. In 2013, it was the Fed's taper talk on top of high oil. In 2018, it was steady Fed hikes plus oil climbing and the IL&FS default freezing domestic credit. In 2022, it was the fastest Fed hiking cycle in decades plus the Ukraine war.

And this time, the oil shock is a supply shock of unusual size. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February 2026, Iran has effectively choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage that much of the Gulf's oil and gas, and a large share of India's, has to pass through. The International Energy Agency called it the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. A ceasefire in April did not restore normal traffic, prices eased over the summer, and then in early October tanker attacks surged again as Iran tightened its grip and America ran a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Layer US yields near their highs on top of that and you have the full pairing. That is why the RBI is defending the rupee with rates and liquidity, not just reserves.

history.title: The embargo, and India's trip to the IMF
history.story:
In October 1973, Arab oil producers led by Saudi Arabia, with its oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani as the face of the crisis, cut supplies to countries backing Israel in the Yom Kippur war. Oil prices quadrupled within months. India, which imported most of its oil even then, saw its import bill explode, and inflation surged through 1974.

Then the Iranian revolution of 1979 delivered a second shock. Finance Minister R. Venkataraman told Parliament in 1981 that two years of rising oil prices had put the balance of payments under heavy strain, and India negotiated what was reported at the time as a record-breaking loan from the IMF. It later chose not to draw the final tranche, a point of national pride.
history.lesson: India's oil vulnerability is structural, not cyclical; it has been there in every decade.

history.title: The airlift and the empty vault
history.story:
When Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the Indians living there were trapped. Over two months Air India flew hundreds of flights, many from Amman after evacuees were bussed across the desert to Jordan, and brought home well over a hundred thousand people. It remains in the Guinness record book as the largest evacuation by a civil airline.

The airlift had an economic shadow: those workers' remittances stopped just as the war sent oil soaring. India's foreign currency reserves drained to a few weeks of imports. By mid-1991, the RBI was pledging gold abroad and the country was on the brink of default.
history.lesson: Oil plus a thin buffer is the classic Indian crisis, and the Gulf matters to India through remittances as much as through crude.

history.title: The IOUs that came due years later
history.story:
By the summer of 2008, crude had climbed to a record. The government kept pump prices well below cost, and the state oil companies ran up enormous losses. Petroleum Minister Murli Deora and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram haggled publicly over how much to compensate them.

The answer was oil bonds: instead of paying cash, the government handed the companies long-dated bonds. The deficit looked smaller that year, but the bill did not disappear. The interest and repayments fell on budgets more than a decade later, and the bonds became a political talking point when fuel prices spiked again in 2021.
history.lesson: Quasi-fiscal tricks shift the cost of an oil shock forward in time; they never remove it.

history.title: The windfall nobody passed on
history.story:
Then the world flipped. From late 2014, a flood of American shale oil and OPEC's refusal to cut output sent crude crashing from over a hundred dollars to below thirty by early 2016. For India it was the best macro news in a generation.

Finance Minister Arun Jaitley chose not to hand most of it to drivers. Between November 2014 and January 2016, the government raised excise duty on petrol and diesel nine times, pocketing much of the fall. The current account deficit shrank, inflation fell and the government used the windfall to repair its finances.
history.lesson: Falling oil is India's single best macro tailwind, and the government, not the consumer, often keeps most of it.

history.title: The relief that sank the oil stocks
history.story:
By the autumn of 2018, crude was climbing, the Fed was hiking and the rupee was setting new lows almost weekly. In September, the infrastructure lender IL&FS defaulted, and credit markets froze. Jaitley's October fuel relief, the story this chapter opened with, landed in the middle of that.

The oil stocks' crash that afternoon was the market saying exactly who it thought would pay for cheaper petrol. They bounced within days as the companies signalled the arrangement was temporary, but the point had been made.
history.lesson: Oil stress and domestic credit stress compound each other, and when the government leans on the oil companies, their shareholders pay first.

history.title: Discount barrels and a windfall tax
history.story:
Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent Brent to its highest since 2008 in March 2022, just as the Fed began its fastest hiking cycle in decades. The rupee crossed eighty to the dollar for the first time. The state oil companies froze pump prices for months.

India found an unusual cushion: while Western buyers shunned Russian oil, Indian refiners bought it at steep discounts, and by October 2022 Russia had overtaken Iraq and Saudi Arabia as India's largest monthly supplier. In July the government imposed a windfall tax on domestic crude producers and on fuel exports, after private refiners had been shipping diesel abroad for better prices while some pumps at home ran dry.
history.lesson: Oil and US rates together is the worst pairing for India; who India buys from can matter almost as much as the price.

history.title: Hormuz
history.story:
At the end of February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran, and Iran answered by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to most shipping. Crude shot past a hundred dollars. In March the government slashed fuel excise to cut the oil companies' losses, and from May the companies began raising pump prices in rounds.

Prices eased through the summer, but the rupee kept sliding to a record in July. Then in October the conflict flared again, with a wave of tanker attacks and an American counter-blockade of Iran's ports, and Brent climbed back above a hundred. The RBI raised rates and opened a dollar window for the oil companies.
history.lesson: A true supply shock is the case India's playbook has least data on, so lean on the mechanism, not on past sector patterns.

today:
Brent is at [[val:brent]] a barrel, up [[val:brent_3m]] over three months: a supply shock, the kind our sector playbook has least data on. The rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar, near its record of [[val:usdinr_record]], and over three months it has moved just [[val:usdinr_3m]]. The rupee is being held, so the pressure is showing up in liquidity and interest rates instead. Meanwhile the US ten-year yield is at [[val:us10y]], up [[val:us10y_3m]] in three months: the worst pairing is fully in place.

Watch four things. Traffic through Hormuz, because that decides whether this is a spike or a regime. Whether pump prices stay frozen, which decides whether inflation or oil company shareholders take the hit. The monthly trade data, especially the oil import bill. And the RBI's reserves and forward book, which tell you how long the defence can run.
sowhat:
In a supply-led oil shock with a defended rupee, almost every link points the same way.

  • Be careful with oil consumers: airlines, paints, tyres, chemicals and the state oil marketing companies while pump prices are frozen. Their costs rise at once; their prices follow slowly, or not at all.
  • Be careful with consumer staples. In our data they lag in every kind of oil spike, demand-led or supply-led.
  • Be careful with wholesale-funded lenders, who pay for the RBI's defence through tighter liquidity.
  • Upstream producers gain on paper, but the government has shown it will tax windfalls.
  • Exporters such as IT services and pharma gain only if the RBI lets the rupee go. While it defends, that cushion stays thin.

What would flip it: shipping through Hormuz returning towards normal, crude falling back, and US yields easing. In that world, oil consumers and staples would be the first to recover, and the RBI could let liquidity loosen again.
